# Education in Sweden
Education in Sweden is structured to provide universal access and is primarily funded and overseen by the government. Preschool is available for all children from age one, with free provision starting at age three for at least three hours daily. Comprehensive school (grundskola) is mandatory for children aged 6/7 to 15/16 and lasts nine years, covering 16 compulsory subjects such as Swedish, mathematics, English, and sciences. Grading begins in year 6, using a scale from A–F, and national tests occur in grades 3, 6, and 9. There are special provisions for Sámi children, students with disabilities, and adult learners (komvux). Independent (friskolor) and for-profit schools operate alongside public schools, funded by municipalities and not allowed to charge tuition or perform selective admissions.
Upper secondary education (gymnasieskola) is elective, with 99% enrollment; it spans three years and is divided into preparatory and vocational national programmes. Eligibility depends on passing certain subjects during compulsory schooling, and all programmes require completion of a diploma project. Higher education is offered through universities and university colleges, with degree cycles compatible with the Bologna Process (bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees). Admission relies on upper secondary school completion, specific eligibility criteria, and proficiency in Swedish and English; the Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT) is also an admission pathway. Higher vocational education is available outside the university system, focusing on workplace experience and specific occupational training. Education is free for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens at all levels, and students can receive financial aid from the National Board of Student Aid (CSN). Sweden monitors anti-discrimination measures in education and handles cases of academic misconduct and grading fairness through government agencies.
